content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. Bemelmans et al. (2010) discussed the implementation of universal access to antiretroviral therapy in Thyolo, Malawi, achieved through task-shifting and decentralization of HIV/AIDS care. This approach demonstrated the potential for improving treatment accessibility in resource-limited settings. 2. Grebely et al. (2018) analyzed phase 3 studies on sofosbuvir-based direct-acting antiviral therapies for hepatitis C virus (HCV) in individuals receiving opioid substitution therapy. The findings highlighted the effectiveness of these therapies in this population. 3. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and other organizations (2017) provided practical guidance for implementing comprehensive HIV and HCV programs targeting people who inject drugs. This document emphasized collaborative interventions to address these infections effectively. 4. WHO's consolidated guidelines (2017) outlined strategies for HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care, focusing on key populations. These guidelines serve as a critical resource for improving outcomes in vulnerable groups. 5. Geboy et al. (2019) demonstrated the utility of leveraging electronic health records to enhance hepatitis C screening within a large integrated healthcare system, showcasing the role of technology in public health initiatives. 6. The WHO Global Update on HIV Treatment (2013) summarized the progress, impact, and opportunities in HIV treatment, emphasizing the importance of continued efforts to expand access and improve outcomes. 7. WHO guidelines (2017) addressed the management of advanced HIV disease and the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy, providing evidence-based recommendations to optimize care. 8. Marquez et al. (2021) evaluated the cost and cost-effectiveness of a real-world HCV treatment program for HIV-infected individuals in Myanmar, highlighting the economic feasibility of such interventions. 9. Brain et al. (2020) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of an outreach model for HCV assessment and treatment facilitation in primary care, demonstrating the value of community-based approaches. 10. Ramachandran et al. (2020) assessed the cost-effectiveness of various care models for hepatitis C treatment in South Australia, providing insights into optimizing resource allocation. 11. Walker et al. (2020) examined the cost and cost-effectiveness of a simplified treatment model using direct-acting antivirals for chronic hepatitis C in Cambodia, emphasizing the benefits of streamlined care delivery. 12. Alavi et al. (2013) investigated the assessment and treatment of HCV infection among people who inject drugs in opioid substitution settings, as part of the ETHOS study, highlighting the feasibility of integrating HCV care into addiction treatment services. 13. Akiyama et al. (2019) explored linkage to hepatitis C care following incarceration in jail through a prospective clinical trial, demonstrating the importance of continuity of care for this population. 14. Zampino et al. (2015) reviewed the epidemiology, outcomes, and treatment of HCV infection among prisoners, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions in correctional settings. 15. Castro et al. (2020) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effectiveness of decentralized delivery of HCV treatment with direct-acting antivirals, underscoring the potential of this approach to improve access and outcomes. 16. Cooke (2021) discussed the role of decentralization, integration, and task-shifting in accelerating the elimination of hepatitis C, highlighting innovative strategies to address barriers in care delivery. 17. Iwu and Holzemer (2014) reviewed the clinical outcomes and self-efficacy of nurses involved in task-shifting HIV management from doctors to nurses in Africa, demonstrating the viability of this approach in resource-limited settings. 18. The WHO Expert Panel Report (2022) emphasized the importance of task-shifting and health system design in optimizing healthcare delivery, particularly in low-resource settings. 19. Hodges et al. (2019) described the successful implementation of a shared medical appointment model for hepatitis C treatment at a community health center, showcasing the benefits of collaborative care. 20. Emdin and Millson (2012) systematically reviewed the impact of task-shifting on access to antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting its role in expanding treatment coverage. 21. Mdege et al. (2013) evaluated the effectiveness and cost implications of task-shifting in delivering antiretroviral therapy to HIV-infected patients, providing evidence for its economic and clinical benefits. 22. Crowley et al. (2021) reviewed ten years of nurse-initiated antiretroviral treatment in South Africa, identifying enablers and barriers to its success. 23. Gilks et al. (2006) outlined the WHO public health approach to antiretroviral treatment in resource-limited settings, emphasizing the importance of scalability and sustainability. 24. WHO's updated recommendations (2021) provided guidance on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation, and monitoring, reflecting the latest evidence-based practices. 25. Vojnov et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the performance of non-laboratory staff in diagnostic testing and specimen collection in HIV programs, demonstrating the feasibility of task-shifting in diagnostics. 26. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (2022) issued public health guidance on integrated testing for HIV, hepatitis B, and C in the EU/EEA, promoting a comprehensive approach to screening. 27. O’Keefe et al. (2018) evaluated a nurse-led pilot program for hepatitis C testing and treatment in rural Cambodia, highlighting the potential of decentralized care models. 28. Tucker et al. (2021) discussed the simplification of hepatitis C service delivery in resource-constrained settings, emphasizing the importance of streamlined care pathways. 29. Zhang et al. (2021) evaluated a simplified service model for decentralized hepatitis C testing and treatment in rural Cambodia, demonstrating its integration into the public health system. 30. Markby et al. (2021) assessed the impact of simplified HCV care on linkage to care among high-risk patients in Malaysia, providing evidence for the effectiveness of this approach. 31. Shadaker et al. (2020) reported on Georgia's national hospital screening program for hepatitis C, focusing on screening and linkage to care for inpatients. 32. Khonelidze et al. (2019) piloted an integrated screening model for HCV, TB, and HIV at the primary care level in Georgia, demonstrating the feasibility of combined disease screening. 33. Tsertsvadze et al. (2020) reviewed the management of hepatitis C in primary healthcare in Georgia, highlighting the progress made in integrating care. 34. Stvilia et al. (2019) reported on the progress in hepatitis C testing and treatment among people who inject drugs in Georgia, emphasizing the importance of harm reduction strategies. 35. Butsashvili et al. (2020) evaluated the integration of hepatitis C treatment at harm reduction centers in Georgia, based on patient satisfaction survey findings. 36. Stvilia et al. (2021) examined hepatitis C treatment uptake among patients receiving methadone substitution therapy in Georgia, providing insights into the challenges and successes of this approach. 37. Tsertsvadze et al. (2020) reviewed three years of progress toward hepatitis C elimination in Georgia, highlighting the achievements and ongoing challenges. 38. Kikvidze et al. (2018) described a harm reduction-based and peer-supported hepatitis C treatment model for people who inject drugs in Georgia, demonstrating its effectiveness. 39. Mafirakureva et al. (2022) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of an intensive care model for hepatitis C screening and treatment among people who inject drugs in Nairobi, Kenya. 40. Ngwei (2019) reported on the successful treatment of hepatitis C among people who inject drugs in Nairobi, Kenya, emphasizing the importance of targeted interventions. 41. Laval et al. (2018) presented a multi-sectoral model to support hepatitis C testing and treatment access among people who inject drugs in Hanoi, Vietnam, at an international conference. 42. The WHO (2015) published a manual for developing and assessing national viral hepatitis plans, providing a framework for strategic planning. 43. Peeling et al. (2017) discussed innovations in viral hepatitis testing technologies and approaches, highlighting advancements in diagnostics. 44. WHO (2022) provided considerations for adopting and using multi-disease testing devices in integrated laboratory networks, promoting efficiency in diagnostics. 45. The WHO (2019) released a progress report on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections, emphasizing accountability for global health sector strategies. 46. WHO (2016) outlined recommended indicators and frameworks for monitoring and evaluating viral hepatitis B and C, providing guidance for program assessment. 47. Govindasamy et al. (2012) systematically reviewed risk factors, barriers, and facilitators for linkage to antiretroviral therapy care, identifying key determinants of successful care transitions. 48. Willenbring (2005) discussed concepts and approaches for integrating care for patients with infectious, psychiatric, and substance use disorders, emphasizing the need for comprehensive care models. 49. Hickman et al. (2008) evaluated the use of dried blood spots for hepatitis C testing among injecting drug users in specialist drug treatment and prison settings, demonstrating its feasibility and effectiveness. 50. Koruk et al. (2011) conducted an intervention study to improve hepatitis B testing and preventive practices in an obstetrics hospital, highlighting the impact of targeted interventions.
